**Long-term impact of digital media on brain development in children** (URL: [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-63566-y](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-63566-y)) 

*(Published Jun 2024\)*

*Authors’ final conclusion:* “In summary, **DM usage, particularly playing video games, does not alter cortical brain development** during the 4-year window, **but social media usage is weakly associated with a decrease in cerebellum volumes**, a trend that was accelerated at later time-points”

*  Aim of study was to “investigate the individual effects of DM usage on structural brain development in children aged 9.9 years … over 4 years, adjusted for age, sex, SES, scanner sites, and genetic predisposition”  
  * Children/tweens were between **9-11 y.o.** (9.9 y.o. avg) at first response to survey, and **were followed for 4 years with 3 data collection visits**  
  * Primary measure was glocal cortical surface area (CSA), noting that [previous research](https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bht357) and trends have strongly shown association between global CSA and intelligence at various ages    
    * Furthermore, since environmental variables like SES [have been found](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2001228117) to associate with surface area and not thickness of the global cortex, the authors selected surface area as the measure here rather than thickness  
  * Also looked at volumes of striatum and cerebellum based on prev. cross-sectional studies  
* Surveyed the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study cohort, with 1462 children who reported (usable) data at three points  
    
* At the first survey (**9-11 y.o.** participants), the **mean est. time spent** on DM **was 0.5 h/day SMS, 0.9 h/day video games, and 2.1 h/day watching TV or videos**  
* Then, “the **estimated time spent** using DM types **significantly increased over 4 years** in the overall cohort and in boys and girls,” showing that digital media increases greatly in prevalence as individuals transition from tweens to adolescents   
  * Highlights importance of teaching SMS, and general DM, skills as children/adolescents get older  
  * **Throughout the entire** 4 year **tracking period**, “**children**, on average, **spent 1.4 h/day using social media, 1.5 h/day playing video games, and 2.2 h/day watching television/videos**”  
    * Boys also spent more time on video games/TV & videos, while girls spent more time on SMS/TV & videos, showing a gap between types of digital media use by sex at this point in adolescence  
        
* The authors observed “a positive association of social media usage and time with cerebellum volumes for a linear term … but a negative association of social media usage and time with cerebellum volumes for a quadratic term.” Overall they concluded that “**children who spent a longer time on social media usage … had a decrease in cerebellum volume**.”  
  * There was “an earlier decline and lower volume at the last time-point” (see graphs a & c):  
    ![figure 3][image1]  
  * They also found that **initial social media use** at the start of the study **wasn’t associated with changes** in cerebellum volumes; **the decrease in cerebellum size was associated specifically with increases in social media use over the 4-year period**  
  * Finally, “excluding time spent on video chatting or texting from social media usage” did not change the direction of observed effects between social media use and cerebellum size over time  
* However, the authors **did not find any significant interactions between SMS use and time w/ the global CSA or striatum volumes**–the cerebellum was the only region affected  
* Interestingly, **children spending more time playing video games experienced an increase in cerebellum volume** compared to those spending less time, differing from the trend with social media (see graphs b & d in graph above).   
  * To me, this **seems to indicate that social media in particular, rather than general digital media, might cause negative effects** if not used in a controlled and responsible fashion (speculative, not mentioned in study)  
* For watching TV & videos, there was no significant interaction found with time and any of the three brain regions (global CSA, striatum, and cerebellum)
